Photo by Joe DelNero, NLR 75007 52 | Advanced Computing Annual Report 2025 Advanced Computing Annual Report 2025 | 53 Designing Alternatives to Rare Earth Elements for Magnetic Materials Rare earth elements are vital for today’s high-performance magnets, yet they are widely dispersed and difficult to extract. To address this challenge, NLR researchers harness two powerful supercomputers— Kestrel at NLR and Perlmutter at the National Energy Research Scientific Computing Center (NERSC)—in a coordinated effort to design and predict new families of ferromagnetic nitrides that could deliver high performance alternatives without relying on rare earth materials. Leveraging density functional theory (DFT)-based workflows, advanced beyond-DFT methods, and NLR-developed structure prediction tools, the team explored crystal structures, stability, and magnetic properties BRIDGING TO THE of transition-metal nitrides. Large-scale configuration sampling enabled the researchers to capture atomic, defect, and magnetic ordering effects, revealing promising candidates in previously underexplored phase spaces. DEPARTMENT OF ENERGY Kestrel’s and Perlmutter’s computing also make it possible to perform extensive Monte Carlo sampling of magnetic configurations, such as those in manganese gallium nitride (MnGaN) anti-perovskites, and to LEADERSHIP COMPUTING 3 refine electronic structure models, including resolving discrepancies in reported band structures like those of cobalt three palladium nitride (CoPdN). This work, recently published in Chemistry of Materials,24 directly 3 supports experimental synthesis and characterization efforts. These integrated computational and experimental efforts, funded by the DOE Office of Science’s Basic Energy Sciences Program, are charting a pathway toward rare-earth-free magnets that reduce dependence on critical materials. Traditional modeling approaches often trade accuracy for scalability or vice versa. To overcome both limitations, researchers used multiple DOE supercomputers including Kestrel (NLR), Perlmutter (NERSC), and Frontier (Oak Ridge Leadership Computing Facility) with funding from DOE’s Office of Science.
